title: A reproducible workflow for isolating and characterizing bacterial endophytes, pathogens, and saprophytic colonizers from tomato fruits
author: Ogofure, Green, et al.

steps.title: Collect and transport tomato fruits
steps.instruction: Purchase 120 fresh, healthy‑looking tomato fruits and 120 soft‑rotten fruits from five randomly selected open markets in Benin City, Nigeria between January and March 2019; transport all samples under aseptic conditions and process them within 4 h of collection.

steps.title: Surface‑sterilize healthy fruits
steps.instruction: Perform two successive sterilization cycles on the healthy fruits:

substeps.instruction: Immerse fruits sequentially in 95 % ethanol, then in 1.5 % sodium hypochlorite, and rinse multiple times with sterile distilled water.
Wash fruits five times with distilled water to remove debris.
Immerse fruits in 70 % ethanol for 5 min, rinse twice with distilled water, immerse in 1.5 % sodium hypochlorite for 7 min, then rinse five times with distilled water.
Plate 100 µL of the final rinse water on TSA as a sterility control; if no growth appears after incubation, epiphytes have been removed.

steps.title: Aseptic maceration and plating of healthy fruit tissue
steps.instruction: Aseptically section the surface‑sterilized healthy fruits using a sterile carpel under a laminar‑flow hood, macerate the tissue, and spread‑plate 100 µL of the macerate onto tryptone soya agar (TSA) plates.

steps.title: Process and plate soft‑rotten fruit tissue
steps.instruction: Aseptically macerate tissue from the margins of healthy and rotten zones of each soft‑rotten fruit, serially dilute the homogenate, and plate 100 µL of appropriate dilutions onto TSA plates.

steps.title: Incubate plates and obtain pure cultures

substeps.instruction: For soft‑rotten fruit plates, incubate for 24–48 h.
For healthy‑fruit (endophyte) plates, incubate for 24–96 h, checking daily for growth.
Sub‑culture any colonies repeatedly to obtain pure cultures.
Preserve each pure isolate on a TSA slant at 4 °C.

steps.title: Perform all isolation steps in triplicate
steps.instruction: Repeat the homogenization, serial‑dilution, and plating procedures three independent times (n = 3 biological replicates) for each fruit‑health category (healthy vs diseased).

steps.title: Extract genomic DNA by boiling lysis
steps.instruction: From a 24‑h broth culture, centrifuge 2 mL at 10,000 × g for 5 min; resuspend the pellet in 200 µL sterile distilled water, vortex, heat at 100 °C for 15 min, then centrifuge at 10,000 × g for 2 min; collect the supernatant as DNA template.

steps.title: Amplify near‑full‑length 16S rRNA gene
steps.instruction: Set up a 50 µL PCR containing:

substeps.instruction: 1 µL dNTP mix (10 mM each; final 0.25 mM each).
1 µL of primer 27F (5′‑AGAGTTTGATCMTGGCTCAG‑3′, 10 pmol, ~0.2 µM final).
1 µL of primer 1540R (5′‑TACGGYTACCTTGTTACGACT‑3′, 10 pmol, ~0.2 µM final).
Add nuclease‑free water to reach 50 µL total.
Cycling: 94 °C 5 min; 30 cycles of 94 °C 30 s, 50 °C 60 s, 72 °C 90 s; final extension 72 °C 10 min.

steps.title: Verify PCR product by gel electrophoresis
steps.instruction: Run 5 µL of the PCR reaction on a 1.5 % agarose gel stained with ethidium bromide; confirm the presence of the expected amplicon.

steps.title: Purify PCR product
steps.instruction: Purify the remaining PCR product by ethanol–sodium acetate precipitation, then resuspend the pellet in sterile water.

steps.title: Sequence the 16S rRNA amplicon
steps.instruction: Submit the purified product for bidirectional sequencing on an ABI 3130xl Genetic Analyzer using BigDye Terminator chemistry.

steps.title: Analyze sequences and assign taxonomy
steps.instruction: Trim the raw sequences, perform BLASTn searches against the NCBI 16S rRNA database, and assign species‑level identities to isolates that show ≥99 % similarity; deposit the final sequences in GenBank and record accession numbers.

description: In total, 120 healthy‑appearing fruits and 120 soft‑rotten fruits were sampled from five independent markets, and the isolation workflow was applied in triplicate for each fruit‑health category. The same four Bacillus species were recovered exclusively from healthy‑fruit replicates, whereas the same ten Enterobacterales species were recovered exclusively from diseased‑fruit replicates across all three biological replicates. The method or approach we employed in the study provided comprehensive molecular and phenotypic characterization of bacterial diversity in tomato (Solanum lycopersicum) fruits from Nigerian markets. Through systematic isolation, 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and pathogenicity screening, we characterized 14 bacterial species representing three distinct ecological groups: (i) four endophytic Bacillus species isolated from healthy fruits that exhibited no pathogenic potential, (ii) four pathogenic species from diseased fruits capable of causing soft rot disease, and (iii) six saprophytic colonizers isolated from diseased fruits but lacking pathogenic activity when tested in planta in healthy tomato fruits. The molecular identification and ecological classification of bacterial isolates from tomato fruits is shown in Table 1. The molecular identification of bacterial isolates from diseased and healthy tomato fruits documents the presence of Bacillus xiamenensis, Bacillus pumilus, Bacillus safensis, Bacillus australimaris, Salmonella enterica, P. carotovorum, Serratia marcescens, Leclercia adecarboxylata, Enterobacter cloacae, Kluyvera ascorbata, Citrobacter freundii, Providencia vermicola, Providencia rettgeri and Proteus mirabilis. The summary of molecular identity and ecological grouping of all 14 representative isolates recovered from tomato fruits (Table 1) documents that soft-rotten tomatoes contained predominantly saprophytic and pathogenic bacterial isolates.
